claims.text: High-entropy alloys generally contain five or more principal elements in near-equimolar ratios.
High-entropy-alloy nanoparticles can be prepared in the sub-100 nm size regime.
Multielement HEA nanoparticles can be uniformly dispersed on a conductive carbon support.
Premelting in HEA nanoparticles preferentially initiates at high-energy surface sites such as edges, corners, and defect clusters.
Chemical disorder and high configurational entropy lower the local cohesive energy at high-energy surface sites.
Lower local cohesive energy reduces the local melting temperature of HEA nanoparticles.
Configurational entropy can contribute to thermodynamic stabilization in compositionally complex high-entropy materials.
Defective turbostratic graphite provides edge-plane anchoring with high binding energy for metallic nanoparticles.
Strong anchoring to defective turbostratic graphite improves the high-temperature stability of supported metallic nanoparticles.
Strong nanoparticle-support interactions raise the local energy barrier to surface-liquid formation.
Strongly supported HEA nanoparticles will begin premelting at a higher temperature than unsupported or weakly supported HEA nanoparticles.
Strongly supported HEA nanoparticles will exhibit less surface-liquid formation than unsupported or weakly supported particles.
Support-dependent premelting effects should be observable between approximately 0.5 and 0.9 times the bulk melting temperature.
Unsupported or weakly supported HEA nanoparticles undergo earlier and more pronounced surface premelting because their surface-energy effects are uncompensated.
Premelting effects are accentuated below 100 nm because of the increased surface-to-volume ratio.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to larger particles or alloys with strong intermetallic-ordering tendencies.
Identical premelting onset and DSC signatures under strong- and weak-support conditions, or homogeneous premelting without preferential surface-site initiation, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
